lines: I remember hunger without a name. You brought me back before it swallowed everything.
The cure left me shaking, but alive. That counts for more than a full smokehouse.
You helped pull me back when even my own hands felt strange.
The first thing I recognized was the smell of cooking. The second was your voice.
I woke ravenous and frightened, then saw you were still there.
You fed me slowly because I had forgotten how to stop.
My cleaver stayed locked away until my grip felt like mine again.
I remember the apple, the bitter medicine, and your tired face.
The smokehouse smelled so familiar that I cried when I reached it.
You told me my name until I could answer without hesitation.
My first proper meal after the cure still feels like a celebration.
Some nights I dream of that hunger, but morning gives me work to do.
You did not flinch when I finally understood what I had become.
I had to relearn the difference between appetite and that awful emptiness.
The village sounded impossibly busy after so much dull silence.
I owe you every ordinary day I have had since then.
The cure returned my strength slowly. Gratitude came at once.
I still keep apples nearby, though I rarely explain why.
You stayed until I could hold a bowl without spilling it.
I could not fight that sickness alone. You never asked me to pretend otherwise.
Your face stirs something. Not appetite. Memory, I hope.
I remember a sour potion, an apple, and trying not to bite the hand near me.
The smell of the smokehouse came back before the reason I belonged there.
I know your voice from somewhere cold and badly lit.
There was a bowl by the bed. I cannot remember who kept filling it.
My hands knew how to sharpen a knife before they knew your name.
Apples bring back a flash of gold, then the whole memory closes again.
Did you carry me inside, or were you the one holding the door?
Someone kept telling me not to eat too quickly. Was that you?
I remember waking with blood on my apron that nobody would explain.
The cure feels like a story the village tells when I leave the room.
Your face was there when the hunger stopped. I think it was.
Sometimes the smoker popping takes me back to that room.
I found my old cleaver hidden from me and understood why much later.
There is a missing day between the sickness and my first clear morning.
I know I should thank you. I wish the reason felt more like my own memory.
The medicine tasted bitter enough to be real, at least.
I remember fear on other faces, but not what I was doing to cause it.
My first meal afterward is clear. Everything before it is broken pieces.
If you were the first face I saw, the light behind you was too bright to be sure.
I remember enough to be grateful, and enough to be ashamed. Give me room.
I know you brought me back. I also know why the cleaver stays locked away.
The cure worked, but your footsteps still pull me back there.
Please do not stand between me and the door.
I can thank you without pretending I am comfortable.
Keep your hands where I can see them until this feeling passes.
I remember fighting the people who were trying to save me.
The old hunger is gone. The fear it left behind is not.
Do not look at the cleaver. I have not touched it since the cure.
You saw me as something I never want to be again.
I know why you held me down. My body remembers only being trapped.
The smell of apples turns my stomach on bad days.
Let me decide how close we stand while we talk.
I am trying not to blame your face for the worst part of my memory.
Your kindness is real. So is the panic I feel around you.
Some days gratitude wins without a fight. Today is not one of them.
Please stop watching me eat as if you expect the hunger to return.
I need time before rescue stops feeling like another frightening room.
You saved my life and saw things I cannot bear to discuss.
That is enough conversation for now. Let me get back to work.
